title: The World's Oil Cushion Is Almost Gone. Exxon Just Warned of $150 Crude.
excerpt: US inventories have fallen for eight straight weeks. Global stockpiles dropped 246 million barrels in two months. The next price shock could arrive by late June.
body:
Global oil inventories are draining faster than markets can replenish them, and industry executives are warning that the world may be weeks away from a second price shock — one severe enough to push crude past $150 a barrel and unsettle financial markets worldwide.

The warning comes four months into the Iran war, which has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz to most tanker traffic. Strategic reserve releases and a sharp drop in Chinese demand have kept prices below $100 so far. But the buffers are running out.

The Numbers

US crude inventories, including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, fell to 791 million barrels in the week ending May 29 — their lowest level since February 2024. Stocks have fallen for eight consecutive weeks, shedding nearly 64 million barrels since the war began on February 28.

The SPR itself stands at 357 million barrels, down from 415 million at the start of March. The Department of Energy has loaned roughly 133 million barrels to refiners and traders under emergency agreements that require repayment with premiums of up to 24 per cent. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Friday that borrowers will add an extra 40 million barrels when the war ends — but "when" remains the operative word.

Globally, observed inventories fell by a combined 246 million barrels across March and April. Iran's crude loadings collapsed to below 300,000 barrels per day in May, down from 1.7 million in March. Cumulative production losses may have exceeded 1 billion barrels.

"We're approaching unheard-of inventory levels. Really, really low levels," said Neil Chapman, Exxon Mobil senior vice president, speaking at the Bernstein conference. He warned that dated Brent could spike to $150 or $160 a barrel if drawdowns continue at the current pace.

The Tipping Point

The risk is not the initial supply shock — markets have absorbed that. The risk is the exhaustion of the cushions that have kept prices manageable.

Three factors have suppressed prices so far: the record IEA-coordinated release of 400 million barrels from strategic reserves, a collapse in Chinese seaborne crude imports to a near-decade low, and a 4 to 5 per cent decline in global oil demand, estimated by Goldman Sachs at 4 million to 5 million barrels per day of demand destruction in April alone.

None of these can last indefinitely.

The IEA release is a finite pool. China's reduced imports reflect both economic weakness and strategic stockpile management, not a permanent shift. And the demand destruction — driven by higher prices themselves — creates a feedback loop: if prices fall on lower demand, demand recovers, and prices rise again.

"Once we move into the back half of June, it is likely that we see oil prices rapidly appreciate," JPMorgan's Data Assets and Alpha group predicted, "unless the Strait of Hormuz throughput normalises to pre-conflict levels."

The Wall Street Journal reported that veteran oil analyst Paul Sankey sees "red lights and bells ringing" as early as this month.

The Cushing Problem

In the United States, the bottleneck is becoming physical, not just financial. Crude stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery hub — the pricing point for West Texas Intermediate futures — are approaching levels where operational problems begin.

"At operational minimum levels, there is not enough oil in a tank to pump out and transfer between tanks," said Jeremy Irwin, crude lead at Energy Aspects. Cushing has a working capacity of 78.4 million barrels but has never dropped below 20 million since the US lifted oil export controls in 2015.

US crude exports surged to a record 5.6 million barrels per day in May as Asian and European refiners scrambled for non-Gulf supply. That export boom has accelerated the domestic drawdown.

What a $150 Barrel Means for India

India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil. Every $10 increase in Brent crude adds approximately $15 billion to the annual import bill. At $150, India's current account deficit would widen to levels not seen since the 2013 taper tantrum, putting further pressure on the rupee and forcing the RBI into harder choices about interest rates and foreign exchange reserves.

The pass-through to domestic fuel prices has been partially absorbed by oil marketing companies, but that buffer has limits. Commercial LPG prices have already risen sharply. Aviation turbine fuel costs prompted the government to announce a Rs 10,000 crore interest-free advance to airlines this week to cap jet fuel at Rs 75.6 per litre for 36 months.

For NRIs, the downstream effects are tangible: higher remittance value as the rupee weakens, but higher prices for families back in India on everything from cooking gas to groceries to domestic airfares. Indian airlines, already operating on thin margins, would face existential pressure.

The Ceasefire That Never Arrives

President Trump has said for days that a deal to reopen the strait is imminent. It has not materialised. Iran has conditioned any agreement on the release of $24 billion in frozen assets and a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Hezbollah's leader rejected the latest US-brokered pact on Thursday.

Meanwhile, fighting continues to flare. On Friday, the US struck Iranian coastal radar sites on Goruk and Qeshm Island after shooting down four drones launched toward the strait. Iran's navy fired warning missiles at US warships in the Gulf of Oman. The IRGC recently struck Kuwait International Airport, killing one Indian national and injuring 63 others.

Even if a deal is reached, RBC Capital Markets noted that restoring energy flows will take months. Mines need clearing. Shipowners will demand hefty war-risk insurance premiums. And global stockpiles will need to be rebuilt — a process that will keep prices elevated long after the strait reopens.

The oil market has been living on borrowed time and borrowed barrels. Both are running out.

Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Goldman Sachs, Energy Information Administration, OilPrice.com
